According to the story, she wished to lie in this spot so that she could guide travellers on Fossavegur, the route that runs south from here to Hnappadalur.
d3292c47-787a-690f-7f7f-591cbf4ad288.story_is: Helguhóll er strýtumyndaður, allsérkennilegur hóll, nokkuð stór, sem stendur í miðjum flóa, rétt við þar sem Stangáin fellur í Dunká. Þarna á Helga Bárðardóttir Snæfellsáss að vera heygð. Er sagt að hún hafi viljað liggja hér til að leiðbeina ferðafólki um Fossaveg sem hér liggur suður til Hnappadals.

d330b513-0b41-af07-590b-6343e92cd64f.story_eng: Félagsgarður, roughly "the society garden" or "the shared garden", was a plot on heathland below the old stekkur (a lambing fold) in Stekkahvammur. In the years 1910 to 1912 several farmers grew potatoes here together as a joint venture. The garden is gone and the land is now hayfield, and the ruins of the fold above it have also disappeared.
d330b513-0b41-af07-590b-6343e92cd64f.story_is: Neðan við Stekkinn í Stekkahvammi var mólendi, og þar var svokallaður Félagsgarður þar sem nokkrir bændur stunduðu kartöflurækt í félagi á árunum 1910–1912. Þar er nú tún, og rústir Stekksins eru einnig horfnar.

d33474e9-4ddb-5194-ab38-2c8c85c6a6e1.story_eng: Haugshlíð is the upper part of the mountainside south of the ravine Skriðugil. Below the water level the same slope is called Stekkjarhlíð. Haugshlíð takes its name from Haugur, a mound (haugur) on Skálabrún. In the spring of 1906 a landslide fell from Haugur and formed a new ravine, Nýja-Skriðugil (New Landslide Ravine), and a new scree, Nýjaskriða, below the foot of the mountain.
d33474e9-4ddb-5194-ab38-2c8c85c6a6e1.story_is: Fjallið sunnan Skriðugils heitir Stekkjarhlíð neðan vatnsborðsins en Haugshlíð ofar, kennd við Haug á Skálabrún. Vorið 1906 féll skriða úr Haugnum og myndaði Nýja-Skriðugil og Nýjuskriðu neðan fjallsróta.

d3664962-313f-0b57-26a2-1afc9b9e9eb7.story_eng: The river is believed to have originally been called Króká. According to oral tradition, a pair of lice-ridden breeches was once found there, and after that the river was called Bróká, from brók, an old word for breeches.
d3664962-313f-0b57-26a2-1afc9b9e9eb7.story_is: Talið er að upphaflega hafi áin heitið Króká. Munnmælasagnir herma að þar hafi fundist lúsug brók og eftir það hafi áin verið kölluð Bróká.

d3ab9961-25ef-46ea-80cf-cbef8cb52d5c.story_eng: Stefanía is the second-largest of the rock outcrops here. On top of it are the ruins of a shelter built by Stefán the shepherd while he sat watching over the sheep. The outcrop appears to take its name from him. The ruin can be seen clearly from the main road, the Krýsuvíkurleið, which passes right by.
d3ab9961-25ef-46ea-80cf-cbef8cb52d5c.story_is: Stefanía er önnur stærsta klöppin. Uppi á henni er rúst af byrgi sem Stefán smali byggði í hjásetunni. Vel sést fyrir rústinni af þjóðveginum, Krýsuvíkurleið, sem liggur þar fram hjá.

d3b1a3b0-0d60-331b-fdda-efe8e0a5ee93.story_eng: Illafit, roughly "the bad meadow", was known for its many bogs and quagmires, which were said to cause accidents. The stream Stóragróf rises at the top of this stretch of land, which lies south of Tunga and runs to the farm boundary.
d3b1a3b0-0d60-331b-fdda-efe8e0a5ee93.story_is: Stykkið suður frá Klappargróf, sunnan við Tungu að merkjum, heitir Illafit. Efst í henni eru upptök Stórugrófar og þar er mikið af dýjum sem slys hljótast af.

d3e42632-0a3d-dcc0-71d1-f238d691bb64.story_eng: Möggubrekka is a fairly recent name. The slope is named after Margrét Gunnarsdóttir, sister of Árni, the farmer at Keflavík, who often picked berries here (Magga is a pet form of Margrét). It lies on the east side of a stony ridge, west of the home field and the old road, west of the old farmhouse.
d3e42632-0a3d-dcc0-71d1-f238d691bb64.story_is: Nafn brekkunnar er frekar nýlegt og kennt við systur Árna bónda í Keflavík, Margréti Gunnarsdóttur, er oft tíndi þarna ber. Möggubrekka er vestan við túnið og vestan við Gamla veginn, vestur af gamla íbúðarhúsinu, austan í grýttum hrygg.

d3eb5f3d-af77-96c4-c4b1-8ef64e0bedb2.story_eng: Grundarhús stood northeast of the farm, a short way west of the present road. It was a beautifully built stone structure, and it is said that it had been placed under protection, yet it was levelled all the same. It belonged to a cluster of farm buildings northeast of the farm: next to it was Valdahús, a sheep house built by the farmer Sigvaldi Pálsson; west of Grundarhús was another sheep house that held 40 sheep; and north of Valdahús stood Harðarkofi, a small horse shed named after the stallion Hörður. Grundarhús no longer exists.
d3eb5f3d-af77-96c4-c4b1-8ef64e0bedb2.story_is: Grundarhús voru norðaustur af bænum og fremur stutt vestan við núverandi veg. Það var fallega hlaðið mannvirki og er sagt að búið hafi verið að friðlýsa það, en samt var það jafnað út. Næst voru Valdahús, fjárhús byggð af Sigvalda Pálssyni bónda. Vestur af Grundarhúsum var annað fjárhús og tók það 40 kindur. Harðarkofi var norðan við Valdahús, lítill hesthúskofi kenndur við graðhestinn Hörð. Þessi hús voru í þyrpingu norðaustur af bænum.

d3ebfa48-5b36-7ca9-10ba-b3fa16c2db66.story_eng: Legend says that Kolur, a wealthy farmer, fell in love with the housewife at Ragnheiðarstaðir and visited her often. The way between them was long and always hard going, across fields and the wide Miklavatnsmýri marsh down to the sea, a walk of at least two hours. To spare himself the effort, Kolur is said to have ordered his workers to build a walkway between his farm and hers. This is Kolsgarður, a considerable earthwork still visible today. It is most prominent beside Langaflóð, where it is quite high. The embankment is about as wide as a well-made meadow causeway, enough for a horse cart, but unlike those, which wind, it runs dead straight. The earth for it was clearly dug from both sides. Southward it points straight at a hill near the sea, believed to be Gömlu-Ragnheiðarstaðir (Old Ragnheiðarstaðir). In 1982 a local man found a fairly thick ash layer from an eruption of Katla, dated to around 1400 or 1500, in the hollow beside it; the ash seemed to have fallen on fully grown-over land, suggesting the embankment is much older. In 1905 Brynjúlfur Jónsson wrote that it was neither a boundary nor a stock wall, and so was probably a walkway.
d3ebfa48-5b36-7ca9-10ba-b3fa16c2db66.story_is: Sagan segir að Kolur stórbóndi hafi komist í kærleika við húsfreyjuna á Ragnheiðarstöðum og sótt á fund hennar oft og iðulega. Er þar á milli löng leið og torfarin alla tíð, þvert yfir Miklavatnsmýri niður á sjávarbakkann, og verður hún tæpast lögð undir fót af góðum göngumanni á skemmri stund en tveimur klukkutímum. Kolur á því að hafa viljað létta sér fyrirhöfnina við að sækja heim ástkonu sína og skipað vinnuliði sínu að byggja gönguleið milli sín og hennar. Þarna er um töluvert mannaverk að ræða sem enn mótar fyrir og er kallað Kolsgarður. Mest áberandi er garðurinn sunnan Langaflóðs, þar nær hann fremst á flóðbakkann og er töluvert hár. Brautin virðist hafa verið svipuð á breidd og vandaðar engjabrýr og nægilega breið fyrir hestvagn. Þó skilur á milli um eitt atriði: engjabrýrnar eru allar meira og minna hlykkjóttar en þessi má heita þráðbein. Auðséð er að efni til garðsins hefur verið tekið utan við hann beggja megin. Garðurinn miðar beint suður í hól niður undir sjó, spottakorn vestur af bænum á Ragnheiðarstöðum, og mun hóllinn vera svonefndir Gömlu-Ragnheiðarstaðir. Sumarið 1982 var athugað hvort öskulag úr Kötlugosi um 1400 eða 1500 sæist utan við garðinn, þar sem efni til hans hafði verið tekið. Var það nokkuð þykkt í lautinni og virtist hafa fallið á algróið land, svo garðurinn virðist miklu eldri. Brynjúlfur Jónsson skrifaði árið 1905 að garðurinn virtist hvorki ætlaður til að vera landamerkjagarður né vörslugarður og því væri rétt að hann hefði verið göngugarður.

d3fca71b-44db-fea2-62da-329f46e026dc.story_eng: The name means Oddný's hillocks. A girl probably perished here, although no story about it has survived. The hillocks lie out on the heath, north of Réttarhólar or somewhat further east.
d3fca71b-44db-fea2-62da-329f46e026dc.story_is: Líklega hefur stúlka orðið til á Oddnýjarhólum, þó að ekki sé nú sögn um það fyrir hendi. Hólarnir eru á Heiðinni, norður frá Réttarhólum eða nokkru austar.

d412193a-5b2f-3592-b9a1-eba10cc88263.story_eng: This was the only water mill in Hegranes. It was built at Keldudalur by Jónas Jónsson of the neighbouring farm Hróarsdalur, whom his son Hróbjartur Jónasson (born 1893) described as a master craftsman, a great worker and always busy. Keldudalur had the only farm stream in Hegranes with enough water to turn a mill. Jónas also built a windmill at home, which ground grain and pearl barley. According to his son, the barley was ground fine for lummur (small pancakes) and coarser for porridge, and rye was ground fine for kleinur, a twisted fried pastry; kleinur made from fresh rye flour were, he said, excellent bread. Another source says the water mill at Keldudalur stood until after 1925 and was in constant use. It first stood out in Kverkin and was later moved onto the home field closer to the farmhouse. The mill no longer exists.
d412193a-5b2f-3592-b9a1-eba10cc88263.story_is: Jónas Jónsson í Hróarsdal kom upp vatnsmyllu á næsta bæ, Keldudal. Hróbjartur sonur hans, fæddur 1893, sagði föður sinn hafa verið „þjóðhagasmið, mikinn verkmann og alltaf starfandi“. Í Keldudal var eini bæjarlækurinn í sveitinni, Hegranesinu, sem var nógu vatnsmikill til að snúa myllunni, og það var eina vatnsmyllan í Hegranesinu. Jónas bjó einnig til vindmyllu sem malaði kornið og bankabyggið. Bankabyggið var malað fínt og haft í lummur, það grófara í grauta, og rúgur var líka malaður fínt og hafður í kleinur. „Ágætt brauð kleinur úr nýju rúgmjöli,“ sagði Hróbjartur. Vatnsmyllan í Keldudal stóð fram yfir 1925 og malaði stöðugt. Fyrst var hún úti í Kverkinni, en svo var hún færð heim á túnið nær bænum. Myllan er nú horfin.

d433d70c-49ea-8311-c23a-948abb6ac84c.story_eng: Kjarnagerði is an old abandoned farm at the foot of the slope, in the southern part of the land of Laugaból (Breiðanes). For a long time there was a beitarhús here, a sheep house out in the grazing land, and quite large wall remains stood until the land was broken up for cultivation. A turf wall was built around the enclosure and kept up until close to the end of the last century. Traces of another wall could also be seen around a much larger area, but it had mostly sunk into the bog before the bog was drained. People lived at Kjarnagerði for a few years late in the last century. There also seemed to be remains of settlement from long before.
d433d70c-49ea-8311-c23a-948abb6ac84c.story_is: Sunnan við Breiðanes, upp við brekkuna, er gamalt eyðibýli sem heitir Kjarnagerði. Það er neðan undir brekkunni, sunnarlega í landi Laugabóls (Breiðaness). Þarna voru lengi beitarhús, og stóðu þar allmikil veggjabrot þar til landið var brotið til ræktunar. Torfgarður var hlaðinn um gerðið og honum haldið við fram undir lok síðustu aldar. Auk þess vottaði fyrir garði um allmiklu stærra svæði, en hann var að mestu horfinn í mýrina áður en mýrin var framræst. Á Kjarnagerði var búið nokkur ár seint á síðustu öld. Auk þess virtust þar vera menjar löngu liðinnar búsetu.

d4500108-d47f-f687-1134-9cd30fe7dced.story_eng: Ærlækur (ær means ewe) is one of a group of streams on the slope at Stórulaugar named after farm animals, together with Lambalækur, Hestalækur and Sauðalækur. It runs a little south of Hestalækur, which lies south of an old potato garden belonging to Stórulaugar. The local informant did not know why the streams were given these names, but noted that all of them could be dangerous to livestock, especially to lambs in spring.
d4500108-d47f-f687-1134-9cd30fe7dced.story_is: Í brekkunni sunnan Lambalækjar er Hestalækur, heldur sunnar en upp af bæ, sunnan við gamlan kartöflugarð frá Stórulaugum. Þá er næst Ærlækur nokkru sunnar. Óvíst er hvers vegna Hestalækur, Ærlækur og Sauðalækur heita svo. Hins vegar geta þessir lækir allir, einnig Lambalækur, verið hættulegir skepnum, einkum þó vorlömbum.

d451fbbf-2edd-4c35-a376-8014a8bf4b42.story_eng: This islet in the pond Bessastaðatjörn is a nesting place for eider ducks. According to oral tradition, Bessi, a farmer at Bessastaðir, is buried in a mound on the islet. Bessahólmi is by far the most common name for it, but it is sometimes simply called Bessi, and both names are probably shortened forms of Bessastaðahólmi, which is also heard now and then. In the time of Ásgeir Ásgeirsson the islet was greatly enlarged towards the south by hauling stones and clods of turf out to it across the ice.
d451fbbf-2edd-4c35-a376-8014a8bf4b42.story_is: Í Bessastaðatjörn er hólmi þar sem æður verpur. Það eru munnmæli að Bessi bóndi á Bessastöðum sé heygður þar. Bessahólmi er langalgengasta nafnið á hólmanum en stundum er hann kallaður Bessi, og er hvort tveggja trúlega stytting úr Bessastaðahólmi, sem stundum heyrist. Í tíð Ásgeirs Ásgeirssonar var hólminn mikið stækkaður til suðurs með því að aka að honum grjóti og hnausum á ís.

d469c73b-4841-aa74-5d1f-265a329fca7f.story_eng: This was once large, good hayland, mostly level grassland, and the hayfields here were counted the main and best mowing land in Fljótsdalur. Sometime around 1909 to 1926 the river Þverá is said to have laid the whole area waste, and it all turned to gravel and silt. The field no longer exists.
d469c73b-4841-aa74-5d1f-265a329fca7f.story_is: Það mun hafa verið á árunum 1909–26 sem Þverá setti þetta land allt í auðn. Var þetta mikið og gott slægjuland og að mestu slétt, og voru það aðal- og bestu slægjurnar í Fljótsdal. Allt var þetta vallendi, nú allt orðið að aur.

d48ee2f1-38a1-44b6-a5aa-b0ae1cd1f94f.story_eng: Egilsgjóta is a cleft in the rocks above the cove Egilsgjótuvogur. It is said that the cleft was once roofed over with timber and that a man named Egill was hidden there. He was later burned for witchcraft.
d48ee2f1-38a1-44b6-a5aa-b0ae1cd1f94f.story_is: Upp af Egilsgjótuvogi er Egilsgjóta. Hún er klettaskora sem sagt er að reft hafi verið yfir og falinn þar maður að nafni Egill. Hann var síðar brenndur fyrir galdra.

d495ddc3-2733-ed6c-86ee-7259c9babe60.story_eng: Tungubakkar, also simply called Bakkar, are fairly steep coastal banks about 70 metres high, made of old sedimentary layers that hold a great many fossils, three to four million years old. The banks also contain coal seams, which were dug by the national treasury, especially during the years of the First World War, 1916–1918.
d495ddc3-2733-ed6c-86ee-7259c9babe60.story_is: Tungubakkar eða Bakkar eru 70 m háir, allbrattir sjávarbakkar, myndaðir úr gömlum setlögum sem geyma sæg af steingervingum, þriggja til fjögurra milljóna ára gömlum. Þar eru líka kolalög sem landssjóður lét grafa eftir, sérstaklega á árum fyrri heimsstyrjaldarinnar, 1916–1918.

d498f006-5468-502e-537e-80abb6b9d83c.story_eng: Fjalarfæri was a simple footbridge over the glacial river Jökla. A board was laid across the river here, and people walked over on it. The name fits, since fjöl means a plank or board. It lay at the front of Dráttarhvammur, a hollow below the farm Skriðusel. For a long time the hollow also had a dráttur, a crossing where people were pulled over the river. The plank crossing no longer exists.
d498f006-5468-502e-537e-80abb6b9d83c.story_is: Fremst í hvammi niður af Skriðuseli við Jöklu heitir Fjalarfæri. Þar var lagt borð yfir og gengið yfir ána. Í hvamminum, sem heitir Dráttarhvammur, var lengi dráttur á ánni.

d4b1b6e5-80bb-4219-801f-3f73ba8ef5e8.story_eng: Goðaborg is a rock shaped like a house, standing at the outer end of the peak Hallbjarnastaðatindur. It is said that Hallbjörn, the settler, walked up to it barefoot every morning to worship his gods. The name means "fortress of the gods". Seen from the farm Hallbjarnastaðir, Goðaborg lies due south, where the sun stands at midday.
d4b1b6e5-80bb-4219-801f-3f73ba8ef5e8.story_is: Yst á Hallbjarnastaðatindi er klettur líkur húsi í lögun og heitir hann Goðaborg. Sagt er að Hallbjörn landnámsmaður hafi gengið þangað berfættur á hverjum morgni og tilbeðið goð sín. Goðaborg er í hádegisstað frá Hallbjarnastöðum.

d4b8750a-aeff-4785-bb81-da2cf37ba9de.story_eng: A spell is said to rest on this patch of grass, and it must not be mown. Attempts to cut it have always ended with broken machinery, and milk cows have died. It will not be mown as long as the present family lives at Skiphylur. The name itself means "spell patch", and such enchanted spots, left uncut for fear of misfortune, are known from farms across Iceland.
d4b8750a-aeff-4785-bb81-da2cf37ba9de.story_is: Það hvíla álög á þessum bletti og það má ekki slá hann. Það hefur alltaf endað með brotnum tækjum og mjólkurkýr hafa drepist. Bletturinn verður ekki sleginn meðan þessi ætt býr á Skiphyl.

d4b9577f-6cd3-05b9-e66a-86bc3d2206d4.story_eng: Mið-Prestakelda, the middle Prestakelda, belongs to the Prestakeldur (priests' bogs). These were three wet, boggy strips running down from the ridge known as Hálsinn to the marshland called Flói. They got their name because some of the priests of Goðdalir took these bogs from the farm Tunguháls and used them for cutting hay. The hay from Flói, and probably also from the Prestakeldur, is believed to have been dried on the nearby hillocks. The northernmost bog on the ridge is now called Ystakelda, and it is surely one of the Prestakeldur.
d4b9577f-6cd3-05b9-e66a-86bc3d2206d4.story_is: Prestakeldur nefndust þrjár keldur sem liggja ofan úr Hálsi og niður að Flóa. Nafnið er þannig til komið að einhverjir Goðdalaprestar tóku keldur þessar undan Tunguhálsi og notuðu til slægna. Á hólunum mun hafa verið þurrkað hey úr Flóanum og að líkindum úr Prestakeldum. Ystakelda nefnist nú nyrsta keldan á Hálsinum og er hún sjálfsagt ein af Prestakeldunum.

d4c1f8c4-3f47-d320-2d93-35a8ca4c6f0a.story_eng: East of the church at Nes there is, or was, a hollow, also recorded under the name Netlutjörn. It was named after stinging nettles, which were probably brought there in the late 18th century. Séra Jón Stefánsson, priest at Nes from 1784 to 1797, is said to have grown the nettles in this hollow and used them for healing. The nettle no longer grows at Nes, but a clump of it survives at Ytra-Fjall and another at Laxárnes.
d4c1f8c4-3f47-d320-2d93-35a8ca4c6f0a.story_is: Austur af kirkjunni er, eða var, laut sem hét Netlutjörn. Lautin var kennd við brenninetlur sem þangað hafa sennilega verið fluttar seint á 18. öld. Sagt er að séra Jón Stefánsson, prestur í Nesi 1784–1797, hafi ræktað brenninetluna í Netlulaut og notað hana til lækninga. Netlan er ekki lengur í Nesi, en þó er til af henni hnaus á Ytra-Fjalli og annar í Laxárnesi.

d4cf7ebd-6c07-6fe0-29a8-69d9d10e7e9e.story_eng: This hollow lies directly above Stóra-Eldborg. According to the old work Landfræðisaga Íslands, more medicinal herbs were found here than in any other place. The people of Krýsuvík call it Hvítskeggshvammur, while elsewhere it is known as Hvítserkshvammur or even Hvískeifuhvammur.
d4cf7ebd-6c07-6fe0-29a8-69d9d10e7e9e.story_is: Í Landfræðisögu Íslands er sagt frá því að í þessum hvammi hafi fundist fleiri lækningajurtir en á nokkrum öðrum stað. Hvammurinn er beint upp af Stóru-Eldborg. Krýsvíkingar kalla hann Hvítskeggshvamm, en annars staðar heitir hann Hvítserkshvammur eða jafnvel Hvískeifuhvammur.

d4e5cee6-3ff8-4aca-13c6-7372fac2a272.story_eng: Oral tradition says that a priest serving the Dýrafjörður parishes fell to his death from this high mountain on his way to the annex church at Sæból, and that the peak has been named after him ever since. The writer of the description thought this very unlikely, since the mountain lies far from any common route. Here it is called Þóroddshorn, and it is also known as Nónhorn. It stands in front of Sandsskarðadalur and served as an eyktarmark for the farm Háls, a landmark by which people told the time of day; nón is the old word for mid-afternoon.
d4e5cee6-3ff8-4aca-13c6-7372fac2a272.story_is: Munnmæli segja að prestur í Dýrafjarðarþingum hafi hrapað fram af fjalli þessu á leið sinni á annexíuna á Sæbóli og sé það síðan við hann kennt, en það er mjög ólíklegt því að fjallið er mjög langt frá alfaravegi. Fjallið er hátt og stendur framan við Sandsskarðadal. Það heitir Þóroddshorn, öðru nafni Nónhorn, og er eyktarmark frá Hálsi.

d4f61ad7-9a10-a06a-1923-a2f33d18b856.story_eng: Tófumýri, "Fox Marsh" (tófa is an old word for fox), got its name because a fox was killed there long ago. It lies to the west of Strákamýri.
d4f61ad7-9a10-a06a-1923-a2f33d18b856.story_is: Tófumýri fékk nafnið af því að þar var drepin tófa fyrir löngu. Hún er vestur af Strákamýrinni.

d4fd6312-58c1-cce8-ebe9-8446f7b5d6a0.story_eng: Nautahvammur means 'bulls' hollow'. Bulls belonging to the people of Þingeyjarsýsla were sometimes slaughtered here when it proved difficult to get them across Vaðlarnir, the shallows they had to cross on the way to slaughter in Akureyri. In the time of Sigríður Harðardóttir the place was usually called Gjáin, 'the gully'.
d4fd6312-58c1-cce8-ebe9-8446f7b5d6a0.story_is: Nautum Þingeyinga var stundum lógað í Nautahvammi ef erfiðlega gekk að koma þeim yfir Vaðlana til slátrunar á Akureyri. Í tíð Sigríðar Harðardóttur var hvammurinn jafnan nefndur Gjáin.

d5049dc8-ef72-4d45-a66a-52f16dbb3b01.story_eng: Halaendar are low cliffs running along the river below the ridge Miðaftansás. Just beyond them lies an old ford across the river called Ketilhlaup, a little in front of the mouth of the stream Jökullækur on its north side.
d5049dc8-ef72-4d45-a66a-52f16dbb3b01.story_is: Út af Miðaftansási eru lágir klettar meðfram fljótinu og heita Halaendar. Utan við Halaenda er gamalt vað á fljótinu sem heitir Ketilhlaup, rétt framan við Jökullækjarós að norðan.

d521ce04-5175-60e4-e013-4e8c6a534ed0.story_eng: Lambegg is one of four distinctive hills known together as Eggjar. It was commonly believed that huldufólk (hidden people) lived there.
d521ce04-5175-60e4-e013-4e8c6a534ed0.story_is: Eggjar heita fjórir sérkennilegir hólar og er Lambegg einn þeirra. Því var almennt trúað að þar byggi huldufólk.

d525e4d1-0a5e-1247-8f5e-5d0de9745f5c.story_eng: In Gyltuholt, a low hill, there is a pit called Gyltupyttur. According to a folk tale, a cauldron of silver or gold lies down in the pit with a large stone slab on top of it. The hill lies beyond the stream Gyltulækur, which flows into the river Apá. All the Gylta names here (Gyltuholt, Gyltulækur and Gyltupyttur) come from old Gylta, the wife of Api, who lived at Neðra-Apavatn.
d525e4d1-0a5e-1247-8f5e-5d0de9745f5c.story_is: Í Gyltuholti er pyttur sem heitir Gyltupyttur. Þjóðsaga hermir að ofan í honum sé silfur- eða gullketill og hella mikil ofan á. Holtið er framan við Gyltulæk, sem rennur í Apá. Öll þessi Gyltu-nöfn eru af Gyltu gömlu, konu Apa. Hún bjó á Neðra-Apavatni.

d5284888-5083-5f45-2179-4235f94a6965.story_eng: Fishermen's huts (sjóbúðir) are believed to have stood here at the time when fishing by rowing boat from the Eyjafjallasandur shore was at its height. The place is also known as Búðarhóll, and the name búð itself means a hut or booth.
d5284888-5083-5f45-2179-4235f94a6965.story_is: Talið er að sjóbúðir hafi verið þar þegar útræði var sem mest frá Eyjafjallasandi.

d535147f-2184-010b-3462-f048ae8d8eb5.story_eng: Brúðgumagjá, whose name means "bridegroom's fissure", is a fissure that has been roofed over with flat slabs of stone, because livestock had fallen into it and died there more than once. One account places it in the middle of the flat rock area known as Hellurnar, north of Sund. According to another account, passed down by word of mouth, it lies to the north in Kleif, beside a stretch of built stone wall that runs up over the Kleif.
d535147f-2184-010b-3462-f048ae8d8eb5.story_is: Brúðgumagjá er gjá sem reft hefur verið yfir með hellugrjóti því skepnur hafa í fleirgang farist þar. Vestan við Helluholt er Sund en norðan við það, á miðjum Hellunum, er gjáin. Munnleg heimild er einnig til um að Brúðgumagjá sé norður í Kleif, við hliðina á hlöðnum veggkafla upp yfir Kleifina.

d53fce49-60b8-ac36-9ec1-0d205398acfc.story_eng: In 1941 every window in the house at Oddi was shattered by an explosion when a sea mine drifted ashore on the beach. The house was taken down in 1942 and rebuilt in Þórshöfn, where it still stands under the name Ásgarður. Nothing of the house remains here.
d53fce49-60b8-ac36-9ec1-0d205398acfc.story_is: Árið 1941 brotnuðu allar rúður í húsinu í sprengingu sem varð þegar tundurdufl rak á fjöruna. Húsið var tekið niður árið 1942 og endurbyggt á Þórshöfn. Þar stendur það enn og nefnist Ásgarður.

d54a5a2b-6c2a-fd8a-4c96-82e25fde8c40.story_eng: An old peat pit where peat, called svörður here, was dug for the farm Arnkelsgerði. Around 1940 a work crew was sent from Eskifjörður to dig peat at this spot for two summers, a consequence of the Second World War. There are more peat pits on Arnkelsgerði land.
d54a5a2b-6c2a-fd8a-4c96-82e25fde8c40.story_is: Gömul svarðargryfja þar sem tekinn var upp svörður fyrir Arnkelsgerði. Um 1940 var gerður út vinnuflokkur frá Eskifirði til að taka upp svörð á þessum stað í tvö sumur. Það var afleiðing af seinna stríðinu. Fleiri svarðargrafir eru í Arnkelsgerðislandi.

d551383e-b52b-7e6c-af2e-e42823272fb1.story_eng: Ófærusker, also called Sperrhólmi, is an islet in the middle of the river. Its name means roughly 'impassable skerry', and it cannot be reached from either bank. It is sometimes counted among the Hofstaðahólmar islets. Even so, Jón á Hofstöðum (Jón of the farm Hofstaðir) is said to have once ridden out to it.
d551383e-b52b-7e6c-af2e-e42823272fb1.story_is: Ófærusker eða Sperrhólmi er í miðri ánni. Það er stundum talið til Hofstaðahólma, en í það verður hvorugu megin komist. Þó er Jón á Hofstöðum sagður hafa riðið í þennan hólma.

d566bb75-5933-cecc-13b2-c4ee6a5e6454.story_eng: Augnlækur was a boggy, treacherous mire lying between two other features, Seftjörn and Stóradæl. A boy is said to have perished there, and the neighbourhood is said to have been haunted ever since.
d566bb75-5933-cecc-13b2-c4ee6a5e6454.story_is: Lækurinn lá á milli Seftjarnar og Stórudælar og var forarfen. Þar átti að hafa farist strákur og verið reimt í nágrenninu síðan.

d579b613-ee33-fd41-aa34-0a8ed6b5ffdf.story_eng: Skiptingar is a dip in the ridges west of the farm Ás. Þórunn Jónsdóttir, who grew up at Ás, and others often saw lights here. The lights were clear but not large, and they were attributed to huldufólk (hidden people). It is said that when a road was being built on Lákabyrgisás, a ridge just south of the farm road and Skiptingar, the workers found that hidden beings would not accept the road being laid where it had been planned. Even the machines are said to have stopped running. A rock outcrop was to be blasted there, but the plan was abandoned and the road was moved a little. Some believe the name Skiptingar, meaning roughly 'the divides', comes from a change in the weather, as the weather is different to the south of the hollow than to the north.
d579b613-ee33-fd41-aa34-0a8ed6b5ffdf.story_is: Þórunn Jónsdóttir, sem ólst upp í Ási, og fleiri sáu oft ljós í svonefndum Skiptingum vestur undan bænum í Ási. Ljósin voru greinileg, en ekki stór, og voru eignuð huldufólki. Skiptingar eru slakki í Ásana þar. Sagt er að í sambandi við vegagerð á Lákabyrgisási, sem er sunnan við heimveginn og Skiptingar, hafi menn rekið sig á að huldar vættir sættu sig ekki við að vegurinn væri lagður þar sem menn höfðu ákveðið. Jafnvel hafi vélarnar hætt að ganga. Stóð til að sprengja þar klöpp, en svo var hætt við það og veginum hnikað til. Nafnið Skiptingar ætla sumir að hafi komið til af veðurbreytingu, þ.e. að annað veðurlag sé sunnan við þær en norðan.

d58763b4-21d6-a504-05e0-6546ee14c210.story_eng: Gerðiskot was a small farm in the home field of Flóagafl, and its ruins are among the largest in the Flóagafl home field. The farm was abandoned in 1915, and its last farmer was Dagur Brynjólfsson. The ruins lie just east of a small dip in the home field called Flóagaflsdæla, east of the Flóagafl farmhouse.
d58763b4-21d6-a504-05e0-6546ee14c210.story_is: Í Gerðiskoti eru tætturnar einna mestar í Flóagaflstúninu. Gerðiskot lagðist í eyði árið 1915 og var síðasti ábúandinn Dagur Brynjólfsson. Tætturnar eru austur af smádælu í túninu, Flóagaflsdælu, sem er austur af Flóagaflsbænum.

d588d718-9c42-805c-26d5-e00e2105dbc8.story_eng: Árneshellir, also called Útilegumannahellir (the outlaws' cave), is linked by oral tradition to Árnes Pálsson, a companion of the famous outlaw Fjalla-Eyvindur. He is said to have stayed in the cave for two years after he fled from Akrafjall. The person who described the cave recalled that when they first came here there were quite a lot of bones in it, but these have all since been removed. A cross is scratched into the rock at the innermost end of the cave.
d588d718-9c42-805c-26d5-e00e2105dbc8.story_is: Munnmælasagnir eru um að Árnes Pálsson, er var með Fjalla-Eyvindi, hafi haldið til í hellinum í tvö ár eftir að hann flúði úr Akrafjalli. Hellirinn er einnig nefndur Útilegumannahellir. Er ég kom fyrst í hellinn var talsvert af beinum í honum en nú er búið að fjarlægja þau öll. Krossmark er rissað í bergið innst í hellinum.

d5923b0d-a167-2a32-28ac-e516164a0868.story_eng: Karl, meaning "old man", is a rock by the mountain southwest of Kerlingin, "the old woman". It is a handsome rock, but it is said to be no match for its wife: it stands much lower and does not have the shape of a person.
d5923b0d-a167-2a32-28ac-e516164a0868.story_is: Karl er klettur við fjallið suðvestur af Kerlingu, myndarlegur en kemst ekki í neinn samjöfnuð við kerlingu sína, mun lægri í loftinu og ekki í mannsmynd.

d59d7a7b-cde3-ee9a-15ff-b704245fdae0.story_eng: The name Kötlulás contains the word lás, which was used for a short descent route down a cliff. A lás was no longer than this: the man going down fastened one end of the rope at the cliff edge and then slid down along it to the spot he was heading for.
d59d7a7b-cde3-ee9a-15ff-b704245fdae0.story_is: „Lás“ var sú sigleið kölluð sem ekki var lengri en svo að sigmaður setti annan enda vaðsins fastan á brún og renndi sér svo eftir honum niður þangað sem ferðinni var heitið.

d5a2a99e-8d16-f63f-d5ca-d51f2242121d.story_eng: Bakkalending was a boat landing on the south side of the river Bakkaá. On a grassy patch on the shore stood Sjóbúð, a fishermen's hut, until the surf carried it away in 1934. Above the hut was a hjallur, a shed for drying fish, and up on the hayfield south of the river stood Bakkhús with its field, Bakkhúsvöllur.
d5a2a99e-8d16-f63f-d5ca-d51f2242121d.story_is: Bakkalending er sunnan við Bakkaá. Þar stóð í torfu í fjörunni Sjóbúð, sem tók af í briminu 1934. Hjallur var upp af Sjóbúðinni og uppi á túni sunnan ár var Bakkhús og Bakkhúsvöllur.

d5a38366-c390-4f5a-827e-c4d7bfaeddd1.story_eng: This well is said to have been blessed by Guðmundur góði (Guðmundur the Good, a 13th-century bishop said to have blessed many springs and wells). The name Gvendarbrunnur means Gvendur's well, Gvendur being a familiar form of Guðmundur.
d5a38366-c390-4f5a-827e-c4d7bfaeddd1.story_is: Brunnurinn var vígður af Guðmundi góða.

d5a62ead-71d8-4fba-a43d-82a7c3f84013.story_eng: Gvendarlækur is believed to have been blessed by Guðmundur góði (Guðmundur the Good, a 13th-century bishop said to have blessed many springs and wells), and the stream carries his name. It runs to the east and south of Gvendarmór and flows down into Skógagróf.
d5a62ead-71d8-4fba-a43d-82a7c3f84013.story_is: Talið er að Guðmundur góði biskup hafi vígt Gvendarlæk. Lækurinn er austan og sunnan Gvendarmós og rennur í Skógagróf.

d5a9d77f-5755-4931-a152-d04d53f82864.story_eng: Behind the ridge Háabrún lies a stretch of marshland known by the single name Flóar, soft bogs with little root to hold them, full of small ponds. At the outer end of the marshes is a lake, Skemmuvatn, and at the far end of the lake rises Skemmuhraun, a stony hill. It is said that Margrét ríka (Margrét the Rich) of Eiðar had a storehouse there for stockfish, which she had brought over from her fishing station at Borgarfjörður.
d5a9d77f-5755-4931-a152-d04d53f82864.story_is: Á bak við Háubrún heita einu nafni Flóar, fullir af tjarnarpollum, rótlitlir flóar. Yst á Flóum er stöðuvatn, Skemmuvatn, og við ytri enda vatnsins er grýtt hæð, Skemmuhraun. Þar er sagt að Margrét ríka á Eiðum hafi átt geymsluskemmu fyrir skreið sem hún lét flytja frá verstöð sinni á Borgarfirði.

d5d2aebd-eea4-85e3-4b57-0d6d8c3f41d4.story_eng: Þömb was once a long, deep, muddy flood-marsh stretching from the foot of the mountain almost all the way to Ferðamannahólar. Water from the mountain collected in it with no natural outlet, so it swelled up in heavy rain and thaws, as an old folk verse describes: 'Its belly was brim-full of water / and wanted to let some go. / The poor old thing, Þömb, / badly needed to pee.' At such times Þömb is believed to have drained out toward Reykjaland. The marsh was overgrown with bottle sedge and water horsetail. Cows waded into it up to their middles to graze, and the lush plants made them give plenty of milk. The marsh was also mown, at least every other year, with the mowers standing in water up to the crotch or waist. It was considered cold and gruelling haymaking, both the mowing and getting the grass onto dry land, but the hay crop was good. Þömb has since been drained and is now just a hollow in the land.
d5d2aebd-eea4-85e3-4b57-0d6d8c3f41d4.story_is: Þömb var áður langt og mikið forarflóð og náði frá fjallsrótunum alla leið fram undir Ferðamannahóla. Í flóðið safnaðist vatn undan fjallinu en það hafði enga náttúrulega útrás. Belgdist það upp í stórrigningum og leysingum eins og gamall húsgangur lýsir: Belgfull var af vatni vömb / og vildi nokkuð missa. / Greyinu henni gömlu Þömb / var geysimál að pissa. En þá mun Þömb hafa fengið útrás fram í Reykjaland. Flóðið var vaxið blástör og fergini. Sóttu kýr í flóðið, óðu það í miðjar síður og flóðmjólkuðu. Flóðið var líka slegið, að minnsta kosti annað hvert ár. Stóðu sláttumenn í vatni upp í klof eða mitti við sláttinn. Þetta þótti kalsamur og erfiður heyskapur, bæði slátturinn sjálfur og að koma grasinu á þurrt land, en slægjan var góð. Nú hefur Þömb verið ræst fram og er aðeins skál í landinu.

d5d5beac-faaf-0b74-ced7-c544ac76dc4b.story_eng: An ancient burial cairn, a grave from the old pagan times, was found here around 1920, after the wind had blown away the soil covering it.
d5d5beac-faaf-0b74-ced7-c544ac76dc4b.story_is: Þar fannst fornmannadys, uppblásin, í kringum 1920.

d5e5f44a-f6af-47e7-8365-3fd93f7f2b9c.story_eng: Huldufólkssteinar, the Hidden People's Stones, are two enormous boulders in the hollow called Leitislág. Huldufólk (hidden people) are beings of Icelandic folk belief said to live in rocks and hills.
d5e5f44a-f6af-47e7-8365-3fd93f7f2b9c.story_is: Í Leitislág eru tveir geysistórir steinar sem heita Huldufólkssteinar.

d60bab30-3863-21c7-aa32-cd5529e96e76.story_eng: Vilborgarbrekka is the slope above the well, below Hellisbjarg. When the lighthouse was built in 1922, the builders lived in tents here. Their housekeeper was named Vilborg, and the slope, whose name means Vilborg's slope, is named after her.
d60bab30-3863-21c7-aa32-cd5529e96e76.story_is: Vilborgarbrekka heitir brekkan fyrir ofan brunninn neðan við Hellisbjargið. Þegar vitinn var byggður árið 1922 höfðust smiðirnir við í tjöldum þarna. Ráðskonan þeirra hét Vilborg.

d618220d-7945-499e-b0c5-8f64d1ce1170.story_eng: Skiphylur, meaning ship pool, is where the ship of Bishop Þangbrandur lay when he tied it to Klukkusteinn, the bell stone.
d618220d-7945-499e-b0c5-8f64d1ce1170.story_is: Í hylnum lá skip Þangbrands biskups þegar hann batt það við Klukkustein.

d61cb330-17fd-4a4c-0a06-7f13dc05bacc.story_eng: Fjallsvað is a ford on the Hafralækur stream, on the old path called Fjallsgata, directly out from the farm. It was the farm ford between Ytra-Fjall and Hafralækur and the usual route to Hafralækur and Garður. It was shallow and good to cross as long as the water stayed at its normal level. A wall was built across here to keep livestock from the pastures north of the stream out of the meadows and home field. There are also stories that the trading route of the Skriðhverfungar, the people of Skriðuhverfi, and perhaps of others, once ran across this ford on the way to the trading post.
d61cb330-17fd-4a4c-0a06-7f13dc05bacc.story_is: Fjallsvað á Hafralæk er á Fjallsgötu, beint út frá bæ. Þar var alfaraleið í Hafralæk og Garð og vaðið var grunnt og gott meðan vatn var í venjulegri hæð. Auk þess að vera bæjarvað milli Ytra-Fjalls og Hafralækjar eru sagnir um að hér hafi fyrrum legið kaupstaðarleið Skriðhverfunga og ef til vill fleiri. Garður var hlaðinn fyrir til að verja gripum úr högum norðan lækjar í engi og tún hér.

d622c586-51d5-cd6c-3d21-79b9d113be8f.story_eng: Oral tradition says that in hard winters or when hay ran short, people from the farm Svínhagi got grazing for their livestock here, which is how Svínhagaból came by its name. The grassland lies between the Selskógur woods and Leyniskargar.
d622c586-51d5-cd6c-3d21-79b9d113be8f.story_is: Milli Selskógs og Leyniskarga, vestur frá Siggastól, eru Svínhagaból. Þar var fengin beit frá Svínhaga í harðindum eða heyleysi, segja munnmæli.

d6311755-d6f2-8849-2fd1-78f06e9ab724.story_eng: Þrælavík, meaning Slaves' Cove, takes its name from a killing told in Landnáma, the medieval Book of Settlements. Lón-Einar and Laugabrekku-Einar fought in nearby Mannfallsvík, and Lón-Einar fell there. Hreiðar, a slave of Laugabrekku-Einar, then chased Lón-Einar's slaves, caught up with them and killed them here in Þrælavík.
d6311755-d6f2-8849-2fd1-78f06e9ab724.story_is: Í Mannfallsvík börðust Lón-Einar og Laugabrekku-Einar og féll þar Lón-Einar. Hreiðar, þræll Laugabrekku-Einars, elti þræla Lón-Einars, náði þeim og vó þá í Þrælavík. Frá þessu segir í Landnámu.

d653de0f-77db-1e5c-42df-dfa3412329f7.story_eng: Bæjarhóll was an álagahóll, an enchanted hillock under a spell, and it was not to be disturbed in any way. It was, however, mown for hay.
d653de0f-77db-1e5c-42df-dfa3412329f7.story_is: Þetta var álagahóll og mátti ekki hrófla við honum, en hann var sleginn.

d658867c-b857-5053-b049-2c4ef6fd2454.story_eng: Dagmálaklettur is a large lava rock standing on a high lava ridge, in full view from the farmhouse door. It was an ancient eyktamark, a landmark used to tell the time of day by the position of the sun; dagmál is the old name for mid-morning. Knowledge of this time-marker had been lost by 1896, though there was testimony that it had been one. The writer of the description recalls that as children they playfully named the rock Grettistak, after the huge boulders said to have been lifted by the strongman Grettir, even though there was nothing behind the name and the rock was far beyond the strength of a troll, let alone a man. The children's name soon fell out of use.
d658867c-b857-5053-b049-2c4ef6fd2454.story_is: Dagmálaklettur er stór hraunklettur á háum hraungarði og blasir við úr bæjardyrum. Hann er fornt eyktamark, sem var glatað 1896, en til var vitnisburður um það. Hér höfðum við krakkar gefið nafn af barnaskap og nefnt Grettistak, þó að það hefði ekki við neitt að styðjast og væri langt yfir trölla meðfæri, hvað þá manns. Þetta féll þó fljótt niður.

d6680c3b-7521-22e6-7a22-7c39aa861276.story_eng: Litlaskarð, whose name means "little pass", is a fairly narrow pass or hollow on the boundary between the farms Þorsteinsstaðir and Brúnastaðir, a short way below the slopes called Selsbrekkur. Water drains into it from Dýjasund, so the ground is damp but grassy, and it gives good shelter from the north wind. Livestock have been caught in the snow here.
d6680c3b-7521-22e6-7a22-7c39aa861276.story_is: Fremur þröngt skarð eða drag á landamerkjum Þorsteinsstaða og Brúnastaða, skammt neðan við Selsbrekkur. Þangað rennur afrennsli frá Dýjasundi og er skarðið raklent en grösugt og gott skjól fyrir norðanátt. Þarna hefur búfé lent í fönn.

d6d3b2a4-e374-b9ca-1ff3-7237ef9c1565.story_eng: Krakahólmi is one of the islets in the river Héraðsvötn that were used both for hay meadows and as nesting grounds for eider ducks. It is also called Krakkahólmi or Krakkavarp, because it was children (krakkar) who first prepared nesting places for the eider ducks there. It was one of the main nesting islets, along with Víðirhólmi and Langhólmi. The nesting has its difficulties, since the river sometimes floods up onto the islets.
d6d3b2a4-e374-b9ca-1ff3-7237ef9c1565.story_is: Krakahólmi er einn af engja- og varphólmunum í Héraðsvötnum. Hann er einnig kallaður Krakkahólmi eða Krakkavarp, því þar höfðu krakkar fyrst búið um fyrir æðarfugl til varps. Hólminn er einn af aðalvarphólmunum, ásamt Víðirhólma og Langhólma. Það eru örðugleikar í sambandi við varpið, að í flóðum vill stundum flæða upp í hólmana.

d6de68e7-2a0c-497c-a9c8-86ed8f1a7f8e.story_eng: This fairly large bog north-east of Tíðaklettur takes its name from the peat pits (svarðargrafir) dug in it, which are probably not very old. Svörður means peat. The area is also simply called Svörður, as in the local saying "ég ætla út á Svörðinn", meaning "I'm going out to the Svörður".
d6de68e7-2a0c-497c-a9c8-86ed8f1a7f8e.story_is: Mýrin er kennd við svarðargrafir í henni, líklega ekki mjög gamlar. Hún er allstór og liggur norðaustur við Tíðaklett. Þar er líka kallað Svörður og sagt: „Ég ætla út á Svörðinn.“

d704cce9-9e1b-108f-d592-4bb559fab08b.story_eng: Beside the old road, where it came up out of Kleifarnar in the land of Mógilsá, there was a stone cairn called Dyngja (a word meaning heap). Anyone passing by was supposed to throw a stone onto it. The cairn no longer exists.
d704cce9-9e1b-108f-d592-4bb559fab08b.story_is: Við gamla veginn, þegar kemur upp úr Kleifunum í Mógilsárlandi, var dys sem nefnd var Dyngja. Þar átti að kasta steini í þegar farið var fram hjá. Dysin er nú horfin.

d70805a1-3f02-8d43-f866-998572a56888.story_eng: Syðriklöpp (Southern Rock) is one of two rock outcrops in Stekkjarholtsklappir, the other being Ytriklöpp (Outer Rock). The farm land is not believed to have any enchanted spots, places where tradition forbade mowing or disturbing the ground. Even so, the grassy hollows among these rocks were never mown. The ground there is smooth and good for mowing, but it was only ever used for grazing.
d70805a1-3f02-8d43-f866-998572a56888.story_is: Ekki eru taldir neinir álagablettir í landareigninni. Þó voru hvammar í Stekkjarholtsklöppunum aldrei slegnir. Þar eru tvær klappir, Ytriklöpp og Syðriklöpp. Þarna er samt slétt og gott að slá, en þetta var bara notað til beitar.

d70a5329-a354-45cf-9a6d-46f1ed0aa8fc.story_eng: Steinaþýfi is a patch of land below the marsh, reaching down to the boundary of Smáratún. It takes its name from a man called Þorsteinn who lived at Ámundakot, the farm now called Smáratún. The ground was once rough and covered in large tussocks (þýfi), but it has since been levelled.
d70a5329-a354-45cf-9a6d-46f1ed0aa8fc.story_is: Neðan við mýrina var skák sem náði niður að mörkum Smáratúns og var kölluð Steinaþýfi. Hún dregur nafn af manni sem Þorsteinn hét og átti heima í Ámundakoti, sem nú heitir Smáratún. Þar var áður stórgert kargaþýfi, en það er nú sléttað.

d7129b24-f777-a1b3-75c8-cd092741e4a6.story_eng: Legsteinaklöpp is an outcrop of columnar basalt from which gravestones were once taken. Its name means "gravestone rock". It lies in the middle of a strip of ground called Legsteinaklapparrindi, which runs from Votuklappir to Lurksbrekka.
d7129b24-f777-a1b3-75c8-cd092741e4a6.story_is: Á miðjum Legsteinaklapparrinda, sem nær frá Votuklöppum að Lurksbrekku, er stuðlabergsklöpp, Legsteinaklöpp, sem legsteinar voru teknir úr.

d712b82f-c0b9-00fc-ab92-c98cec4e011f.story_eng: Svikahóll, roughly "the hill of deceit", is a round-topped hill with a gravel patch on its summit, lying directly east of the Leifsstaðabjörg cliffs on the farm Leifsstaðir. The view from it seems very good at first glance, but it can badly deceive, because there are hidden hollows close by that cannot be seen from the top. This is how the hill got its name.
d712b82f-c0b9-00fc-ab92-c98cec4e011f.story_is: Beint austur af Leifsstaðabjörgum og beint norður af Moldgili er kollóttur hóll og melur efst á honum. Hóllinn heitir Svikahóll. Sýn af honum, sem í fljótu bragði virðist mjög góð, getur svikið illilega. Því valda leyningar í næsta nágrenni.

d7347970-eb2a-3aca-79d2-014823c52ece.story_eng: Þinghústóft (also called Þinghúsatóft), "the assembly house ruin", was the name of a ruin in the home field at Kópavogur, east of Þinggerði. Beside it lay a stone called Höggsteinn. The stone was moved away in the latter half of the 19th century.
d7347970-eb2a-3aca-79d2-014823c52ece.story_is: Þinghústóft (Þinghúsatóft) var tóft nefnd í túninu í Kópavogi, austan við Þinggerði. Hjá Þinghústóft lá steinn sem nefndur var Höggsteinn. Steinn þessi var fluttur burt á seinni hluta 19. aldar.

d76004f2-125c-1b87-cde8-bcf08247ac4f.story_eng: Grundir was settled around 1650 as a hjáleiga, a small tenant croft belonging to the farm Láganúpur. In 1930 it became the property of the people living there, and it stayed inhabited until 1945. Life at Grundir depended on fishing from the sea at least as much as on farming. While the neighbouring croft of Grundabakkar was still lived in, the two places were in effect one double farm.
d76004f2-125c-1b87-cde8-bcf08247ac4f.story_is: Grundir byggðust sem hjáleiga frá Láganúpi um 1650. Þær urðu eign ábúanda 1930 og voru í byggð til 1945. Búseta byggðist ekki síður á sjósókn en búskap. Í raun var þar tvíbýli meðan búið var á Grundabökkum, þar hjá.

d761b9f3-e183-d453-bf72-7c63dcaecb4a.story_eng: Fardagafossbrún is an edge above Snasir. In it stands the rock Fardagafossklettur, split by the river Miðhúsaá, which forms a fairly high waterfall there, Fardagafoss. Beneath the waterfall is a rock shelter, now partly collapsed. According to folk tales, a skessa (a troll woman) is said to have lived there.
d761b9f3-e183-d453-bf72-7c63dcaecb4a.story_is: Í Fardagafossbrún, ofan við Snasir, er Fardagafossklettur, klofinn af Miðhúsaánni, og myndast þar allhár foss, Fardagafoss. Undir fossinum er hellisskúti, nokkuð hruninn. Þar mun hafa búið skessa samkvæmt þjóðsögum.

d76a2c57-b480-4831-bf7f-1e85afd9bac9.story_eng: At the north end of Stapafell stand two rock pillars. Seen from the sea they are called Strákar (the Boys), but on land they are known as Strípar. Viewed from the east, one of the rocks looks like a troll turned to stone. Its hairdo is a cluster of little pigtails, like the ones Björg Guðmundsdóttir has adorned herself with.
d76a2c57-b480-4831-bf7f-1e85afd9bac9.story_is: Í norðurenda Stapafells eru tveir klettastrípar, nefndir Strákar séðir utan af sjó en Strípar á landi. Einn kletturinn er austan frá séð eins og steinrunnið tröll og skartar hárbúnaði sem er þyrping af tíkarspenum, líkum þeim sem Björg Guðmundsdóttir hefur skreytt sig með.

d78340cd-3b36-a450-bf55-0c0d99ed44e0.story_eng: It is said that Guðmundur ríki (Guðmundur the Powerful) of Möðruvellir had his men build this wall; some say it was his slaves who built it. The wall has now almost sunk into the ground, but traces of it can still be seen by the river and a short way up the hillside. The name means "bull wall" or "cattle wall".
d78340cd-3b36-a450-bf55-0c0d99ed44e0.story_is: Sagt er að Guðmundur ríki á Möðruvöllum hafi látið menn sína, sumir segja þræla sína, hlaða garðinn. Garðurinn er nær horfinn í jörðu, en þó sér fyrir honum við ána og spölkorn upp í hlíðina.

d78d8bae-9047-0cda-cc43-754fb1e2b240.story_eng: According to Landnáma, the Icelandic Book of Settlements, this cove was the scene of a fight between two men, Lón-Einar and Laugabrekku-Einar, and Lón-Einar fell here. The name fits the story: mannfall means the loss of men in battle. Afterwards Hreiðar, a slave of Laugabrekku-Einar, chased Lón-Einar's slaves, caught them and killed them at Þrælavík, the Slaves' Cove.
d78d8bae-9047-0cda-cc43-754fb1e2b240.story_is: Í Mannfallsvík börðust Lón-Einar og Laugabrekku-Einar og féll þar Lón-Einar. Hreiðar, þræll Laugabrekku-Einars, elti þræla Lón-Einars, náði þeim og vó þá í Þrælavík. Frá þessu segir í Landnámu.

d791f99e-91ca-f6a4-69c7-dfa0465cd6e6.story_eng: A fairly large branch of the river flows right along the foot of these slopes. A long time ago there was a sizeable bank, or banks, here, known as Steinsstaðabakkar, but the river, called Vötnin (the Waters), broke them down, and since then there have been hardly any banks left.
d791f99e-91ca-f6a4-69c7-dfa0465cd6e6.story_is: Fyrir alllöngu síðan var hér allmikill bakki eða bakkar, sem nefndir voru Steinsstaðabakkar. En Vötnin brutu þá niður og síðan hafa nánast engir bakkar verið þar, enda fellur allmikil kvísl þar fast meðfram brekkunum, Steinsstaðabrekkum.

d79bd29d-bb75-2c90-3f09-8f5dd1fe0c64.story_eng: Hannesarklettar (Hannes's Cliffs) are two bands of rock on the eastern side of Múlinn, with a path running between them that can be walked. A raven used to nest in the upper band. No one knows who this Hannes was. In front of the cliffs is a cleft in the rock called Hannesarklauf or Hannesarklettarauf.
d79bd29d-bb75-2c90-3f09-8f5dd1fe0c64.story_is: Hannesarklettar nefnast klettar austan í Múlanum, eða tvö klettabelti, og má ganga eftir stíg á milli þeirra. Hrafninn átti hreiður í efra beltinu. Ekki er vitað hver þessi Hannes var. Hannesarklauf eða Hannesarklettarauf er klettaklauf framan við Hannesarkletta.

d7b20b19-f7bd-9cf4-3cc0-0c0464f4984e.story_eng: Dimmikrókur, whose name means "the dark nook", is where the ravine is at its narrowest. A troll woman is said to have lived here. When she heard the holy ringing of the bells of the first church at Ásólfsskáli, she leapt from here out into Tröllagil (Troll Ravine) on Núpsheiði. Others say that a farmer from Ásólfsskáli killed her when she was stuck in a bog with a whale calf on her back and asked him for help, and that he became an unlucky man because of it.
d7b20b19-f7bd-9cf4-3cc0-0c0464f4984e.story_is: Dimmikrókur heitir þar sem gilið er þrengst. Þar voru heimkynni tröllkonu sem stökk þaðan út í Tröllagil á Núpsheiði er hún heyrði helgan klukknahljóm fyrstu kirkjunnar á Ásólfsskála. Aðrir segja að bóndi á Ásólfsskála hafi banað henni er hún var föst í dýi með hvalkálf á bakinu og bað hann hjálpar, en ógæfumaður varð hann fyrir vikið.

d7bd9597-c059-806f-a145-9e3e8350974c.story_eng: Ranghali is a long tongue of lava riddled with caves, running along the foot of the slope at the top of the lava field. Its many caves open in all directions. Near the middle of the ridge are two caves called Hringhellar, which are thought to have once been joined. Sheep were sometimes sheltered in them in autumn and into the winter, and together they could hold up to 200 sheep.
d7bd9597-c059-806f-a145-9e3e8350974c.story_is: Upp við brekkuna efst í hrauninu er hellarani sem heitir Ranghali. Þar eru hellar margir með opum á ýmsa vegu. Nálægt miðju ranans eru tveir hellar sem heita Hringhellar, og munu þeir áður hafa náð saman. Þar var fé stundum hýst á haustin og fram eftir vetri, og taka þeir allt að 200 fjár.

d7bffd75-e418-483e-8218-daf2dd8e1c6e.story_eng: Grásteinn, whose name means grey stone, is recorded as an álagablettur: a spot under a spell. In Icelandic folk belief, such places were not to be disturbed, or misfortune would follow.

d7d59b5f-decb-da5c-cf33-eb609234b8f5.story_eng: Beneath the mountainside, a little north of Fjarðarhorn, lay a small patch of grassy lowland, hard ground scattered with boulders that had fallen from the cliffs above. One huge boulder drew particular attention, because it rested on two stones standing somewhat above the ground, as if it had been lifted up onto them, and it was possible to crawl underneath it. The name of the place is probably connected with these scattered boulders, or "Grettistök", a term for great stones said to have been lifted by Grettir the Strong of the sagas.
d7d59b5f-decb-da5c-cf33-eb609234b8f5.story_is: Undir fjallshlíðinni norðan til við Fjarðarhorn var lítils háttar grasi vaxið undirlendi, staksteinóttur harðbali vegna grjóthruns úr klettunum. Eitt stóreflis bjarg vakti einkum athygli, því að það hvíldi á tveimur steinum sem standa nokkuð upp úr jörðu, eins og því hefði verið lyft upp á þá, og mátti skríða undir steininn. Nafnið á plássinu stendur sennilega í sambandi við þessa staksteina eða „Grettistök“.

d7f4b0f4-66ff-a225-9eef-aef3f692926d.story_eng: Lækjarhúsið was a meeting house built by the local district (hreppur), and it also served as a school. It was probably built between 1923 and 1926, of turf and timber. Turf walls stood on the north and east sides and rose up to the window on the south side, while the west side was of timber and held the door. Inside was a single hall downstairs with a small entrance hall, and a loft above. The timber came from Sæmundarbúð at Kolkuós. According to the local history of Skagafjörður, the singer Stefán Íslandi made his singing debut in Lækjarhúsið on 26 December 1924, the second day of Christmas. The house was finally torn down some time after 1955, and its timber was used for an addition to the baðstofa (the main living room) at Bakki. No trace of its foundations can be seen today.
d7f4b0f4-66ff-a225-9eef-aef3f692926d.story_is: Hreppurinn byggði Lækjarhúsið sem fundahús og einnig var þar skóli. Líklega er það byggt á árunum 1923 til 1926. Húsið var byggt af torfi og timbri. Það var torfveggur að norðan og austan og upp að glugga að sunnan, en vesturhliðin úr timbri. Þetta var einn salur niðri og lítil forstofa. Dyrnar voru að vestan á timburhliðinni. Svo var loft yfir. Viðurinn var úr Sæmundarbúð í Kolkuósi. Í Byggðasögu Skagafjarðar segir að frumraun Stefáns Íslandi í söng hafi verið í Lækjarhúsinu á annan í jólum 1924. Húsið var loks rifið eftir 1955 og byggt úr viðunum eitthvað við baðstofuna á Bakka. Ekki eru sjáanleg merki eftir grunn hússins.

d80b71fb-7750-6e04-f2ea-73b9f8430ca1.story_eng: The story goes that a certain Jörundur, a convicted criminal, was to win his life by leaping across this cleft. The jump failed, and he fell to his death. It was once possible to walk down Jörundarskora to Árhöfn, but in an extremely heavy surf the soil beneath the cleft was swept away, and today there is a sheer 20-metre cliff there.
d80b71fb-7750-6e04-f2ea-73b9f8430ca1.story_is: Sagan segir að Jörundur nokkur, sakamaður, hafi átt að vinna sér til lífs að stökkva yfir skoruna. Stökkið misheppnaðist með þeim afleiðingum að hann hrapaði til bana. Áður var hægt að ganga Jörundarskoru niður í Árhöfn, en í aftakabrimi sópaðist jarðvegur burt undan skorunni og í dag er þar 20 m þverhnípt bjarg.

d80d4caa-1f06-6e51-7ead-d6850ac268b6.story_eng: Remains of a building once stood here, a distinct ruin that was pushed under the road when the road was built, so nothing of it can be seen today. The ruin lay beside a wall that ran along the line of the present road and on to where the farm stands now.
d80d4caa-1f06-6e51-7ead-d6850ac268b6.story_is: Þarna voru leifar, greinileg tóft sem var ýtt undir veginn þegar hann var byggður. Tóftin lá við garð sem fór meðfram veginum eins og hann er í dag og að núverandi bæjarstæði.

d80f8e49-38ef-4e55-9dbe-1ecc2d1c340d.story_eng: Álfaberg means "elf rock". It is the southern end of a long, unusual ridge that runs almost out to Laxárvatn lake. Here the ridge becomes a rocky hill with a low, sheer rock face to the east, grassy on top and crowned by a kind of knoll. Old people once spoke of lights having been seen by the rock, but no story about it was ever written down.
d80f8e49-38ef-4e55-9dbe-1ecc2d1c340d.story_is: Sérkennilegur langur ás nær næstum út að Laxárvatni, þar sem hann lækkar og endar í mýri skammt þaðan. Sunnan til verður hann að klettaholti með lágt standberg móti austri, grasi vaxið að ofan og þar efst með nokkurs konar hól, og heitir það Álfaberg. Gamalt fólk talaði eitt sinn um það að þar hefðu sést ljós við bergið, en sögn um það er hvergi til skráð.

d80fd6bd-d9f2-61b4-9d68-eb264451e95a.story_eng: Hreggnesi is a low rocky point where the sea cliffs begin. There are places called Hreggnasi all over Iceland, but this one is probably the only one spelled with two e's. Hreggur means foul weather, and it can indeed blow hard here in westerly and northerly storms.
d80fd6bd-d9f2-61b4-9d68-eb264451e95a.story_is: Lágt klettanef þar sem sjávarklettarnir byrja utan við Brunnsbrekku. Víða um land eru hreggnasar, en þessi er líklega sá eini sem hefur tvö e í nafni sínu. Hreggur merkir óveður, enda getur nokkuð sviðrað þarna í vestan- og norðanveðrum.

d81bc85e-cfdb-a22e-a78d-2b4245dc5657.story_eng: Molduflöt is a level, grassy flat on even ground where the Ásar hills come to an end, just west of Stekkatún. It took its name from a dun-coloured (moldótt) mare that foaled there. A cluster of greenhouses has since been built on the flat, and it bears the same name.
d81bc85e-cfdb-a22e-a78d-2b4245dc5657.story_is: Slétt valllendisflöt vestan við Stekkatún heitir Molduflöt. Hún er á jafnsléttu, þar sem Ásunum lýkur. Molduflöt var kennd við moldótta meri sem kastaði þar. Á flötinni er nú búið að reisa gróðurhúsasamstæðu sem ber sama nafn.

d8216bde-7b9b-6b5b-5d5e-13895a646e3f.story_eng: Gamlasel, "the old shieling", lies on the south side of Selhóllinn, in a hollow where ruins of old buildings remain. A sel was a summer shieling where livestock were kept and milked. Brushwood must not be taken from this place. Gísli Magnússon, the farmer at Krókur, once did so, and that same year the farmer at Ölfusvatn, Gísli Þórðarson, lost four head of large livestock. This was blamed on the ancient spell laid on the place.
d8216bde-7b9b-6b5b-5d5e-13895a646e3f.story_is: Gamlasel er undir Selhólnum að sunnan. Þar er hvammur með tóftum. Þar má ekki taka hrís. Varð Gísla Magnússyni, bónda í Króki, það á og varð það til þess að ábúandinn á Ölfusvatni, Gísli Þórðarson, missti fjóra stórgripi þetta sama ár, og var það kennt álögunum fornu.

d8243ec1-0710-48dd-ccdf-d7788c100066.story_eng: Gránunes takes its name from a grey cow that went missing and was later found here, having given birth to her calf. Grána is a common old name for a grey cow, and nes means headland. The headland lies beside the cove Stórhólsvogur, and the shallow just off it is called Gránunesgrunn.
d8243ec1-0710-48dd-ccdf-d7788c100066.story_is: Gránunes dregur nafn af grárri kú, sem tapaðist og fannst þarna borin. Nesið er austan við Húsandarklett hjá Stórhólsvogi, og þar fram af er Gránunesgrunn.

d82503af-cad5-527d-8a20-5188324f14c4.story_eng: Tunga, meaning "tongue", was a three-cornered strip of the home field, which sloped noticeably south and southeast from the farmhouse down to the stream. It was bounded by the stream, the vegetable garden wall and a path running southwest from the farmyard to the stream. Where the path came closest to the stream there was an old stone hearth, used in spring when the wool was washed.
d82503af-cad5-527d-8a20-5188324f14c4.story_is: Túninu hallaði talsvert frá bænum suður og suðaustur að læknum. Þar var þrístrend spilda, kölluð Tunga, sem takmarkaðist af læknum, sáðgarðinum og götu sem lá af hlaðinu suðvestur að læknum. Þar sem gatan lá næst læknum voru hlóðir sem notaðar voru þegar ull var þvegin á vorin.

d8350f9b-d034-8c1f-2709-2592aa0aff0c.story_eng: Stekkjarnes is a fairly large, flat and level stretch of land beside the Affall river that was used for haymaking. The name means 'fold headland', stekkur being a small pen where lambs and ewes were kept. At its southern end, just north of where the Affall swings sharply west, are the remains of a sheep fold. The grass-grown walls are still clearly visible. The fold measured about 10 by 15 metres, and a guiding wall for driving sheep into it ran north from its eastern wall. People remembered sheep being sheared in this fold, though later the sheep were driven home to the farm for shearing instead. East of the headland there may once have been river channels.
d8350f9b-d034-8c1f-2709-2592aa0aff0c.story_is: Stekkjarnes er allstórt, flatt og slétt hólmaland og er heyskaparland. Syðst á Stekkjarnesinu, norðan við þar sem Affallinn tekur á sig mikinn sveig til vesturs, eru leifar af rétt og eru veggirnir vel greinilegir, vallgrónir. Stærð réttarinnar er 10 x 15 metrar og innrekstrargarður liggur til norðurs frá austurvegg. Menn muna eftir rúningi í þessari rétt, en seinna var féð rekið heim til rúnings. Austan Stekkjarness hafa hugsanlega verið farvegir út með Holtsendanum.

d85250af-4399-1dfb-70db-12734c583d27.story_eng: The story told of this place concerns Signý, the mother of Hörður Grímkelsson. On her way to her own wedding she stayed overnight at Þverfell, and during the night her riding horse, Svartfaxi, ran off. In the morning he was found dead in a sinkhole up on the ridge. The name Faxaflói carries the horse's name.
d85250af-4399-1dfb-70db-12734c583d27.story_is: Móðir Harðar Grímkelssonar hét Signý. Hún gisti á Þverfelli er hún var að fara til brúðkaups síns og missti þar reiðhest sinn, Svartfaxa, sem strokið hafði um nóttina og fannst dauður í jarðfalli uppi á hálsinum um morguninn.

d85ab22f-63d4-a312-a0cb-aa3b86848be6.story_eng: Smérhellissvelti is a small ledge at the lower edge of the scree below the cave Smérhellir. It is possible to squeeze down onto the ledge, but it is a precarious move. Sheep are believed to have once become stranded there, unable to get off. A svelti is a ledge of this kind, where trapped sheep risked starving, and that is how the place got its name.
d85ab22f-63d4-a312-a0cb-aa3b86848be6.story_is: Lítill stallur í neðri brún skriðunnar undir Smérhelli. Unnt er að smeygja sér niður í sveltið, en tæpt er það. Þar munu kindur einhvern tíma hafa lent í svelti.

d85ebdb2-0562-40a5-aa55-125ea5a90815.story_eng: This pool in the river, just below the ford Efstavað, takes its name from Gunnar, a merchant at Rangá, who practised swimming here. This is believed to have been around 1890, a time when few people knew how to swim.
d85ebdb2-0562-40a5-aa55-125ea5a90815.story_is: Hylur í ánni neðan við Efstavað. Tilefni nafnsins er að kaupmaður á Rangá, Gunnar, æfði þar sund. Það mun hafa verið um 1890, en þá var sundkunnátta fágæt.

d85f68fc-3e9e-833b-62fb-e5c113ebd600.story_eng: This knoll takes its name from Brandshús, a sheep house that once stood here, on a knoll just south of Fitin. A man named Guðbrandur, nicknamed Draugabrandur (Ghost-Brandur), is the subject of a folk tale. He was the father of Bóthildur, wife of Þórður Björnsson, the district magistrate at Garður. Guðbrandur spent his last years at Garður, presumably in his daughter's care. He is believed to have owned a few sheep and kept them in this hut, and he is said to have met a sudden, violent end there. After that, the house was rumoured to be haunted.
d85f68fc-3e9e-833b-62fb-e5c113ebd600.story_is: Brandshúsahóll er kenndur við hús sem stóðu þar. Á hól sunnan undir Fitinni stóðu fjárhús sem kölluð voru Brandshús. Guðbrandur hét maður og var auknefndur Draugabrandur og er til þjóðsaga þar um. Hann var faðir Bóthildar, konu Þórðar Björnssonar sýslumanns í Garði. Síðustu æviár sín bjó Guðbrandur í Garði, væntanlega í skjóli dóttur sinnar. Guðbrandur mun hafa átt einhverjar kindur og haft þær í kofa þessum, og er sagður hafa endað þar líf sitt með sviplegum hætti. Lék það orð á að reimt væri í húsinu eftir það.

d874806e-e537-04ad-802b-ea144f3b84e0.story_eng: There was a sel here in earlier centuries, a summer shieling where livestock were kept and milked. People were living at the place around the time the witch-hunts swept through Árneshreppur.
d874806e-e537-04ad-802b-ea144f3b84e0.story_is: Þarna hefur verið sel fyrr á öldum og þar var búið um það leyti er galdraofsóknir gengu yfir í Árneshreppi.

d8b396e7-3c59-4d74-864d-15f259239d11.story_eng: Ketilbjarnarrúst is a long mound of stones lying in the marshy flat between Hríshóll and Hafrafell. It is said that a man named Ketilbjörn lies buried there, and the place bears his name: Ketilbjörn's ruin.
d8b396e7-3c59-4d74-864d-15f259239d11.story_is: Í flóanum milli Hríshóls og Hafrafells er löng grjótrúst sem kölluð er Ketilbjarnarrúst, og er sagt að Ketilbjörn sé þar heygður.

d8c15dd5-bdab-efe8-b178-cce9f6490653.story_eng: There was once a dráttur, a cable crossing with a kláfur (a basket or box hung from a cable), on this bank for crossing the glacial river Jökla. The bank is down on the riverbanks below the farm, a little further out than the old Nátthagi (night pasture) and close to Heimagróf.
d8c15dd5-bdab-efe8-b178-cce9f6490653.story_is: Þar var dráttur, eða kláfur, yfir Jöklu. Bakkinn er niðri á bökkunum fyrir neðan bæinn, nokkuð utar en þar sem Nátthagi var, og er út undir Heimagróf.

d8c4585a-4bfb-a41f-40c8-4c953a785ce9.story_eng: Borgarvíkurtangi was once a point of land jutting out into the lake in the middle of Borgarvík bay. When the water level rose, it became an islet and some of the land went under water. There was good peat-cutting here, but it can no longer be used because the water is now so high.
d8c4585a-4bfb-a41f-40c8-4c953a785ce9.story_is: Borgarvíkurtangi skagaði út í vatnið í miðri Borgarvíkinni en þegar hækkaði í vatninu varð hann að hólma og nokkuð af landi fór í kaf. Þar var gott mótak sem nú er ekki hægt að nota vegna þess hvað hátt er í vatninu.

d8d01a42-2336-6000-978c-a7300878b37d.story_eng: Bleikslág is a rocky gully in the edge of Hofin. The name comes from an event early in the 19th century, when a pale yellowish-dun colt (bleikur) fell to its death here. The colt was considered a great loss, and the gully has been named after it ever since.
d8d01a42-2336-6000-978c-a7300878b37d.story_is: Bleikslág er klettagil í brún Hofanna. Nafnið er þannig til komið að snemma á 19. öldinni hrapaði þar bleikur foli sem mikil eftirsjá var talin í, og er gilið við folann kennt síðan.

d8d2c99c-13a9-dc5d-66de-1f98f978a3e8.story_eng: Hvarf is a hollow on the side of a gravel ridge. The crossing is only a few fathoms wide, yet it was the very worst and most fearsome spot in the area. The mud slope is extremely steep, and there was hardly any chance of finding a foothold or a handhold if anyone strayed off the path. The path itself could be dangerously narrow, because mud tended to slide down into it from the slope above. People always tried to shovel it clear for both people and animals in summer and while the ground was unfrozen. Traffic over it was heavy, since cows and horses were kept in Skriðurnar, where there was fairly good grazing. In winter people often went higher up, just below the cliffs, to avoid the danger of avalanches.
d8d2c99c-13a9-dc5d-66de-1f98f978a3e8.story_is: Utan í melhrygginn er hvilft sem heitir Hvarf. Það er aðeins nokkra faðma yfir að fara en þó alversti og ægilegasti staður á þessum slóðum. Aurskriðan er snarbrött og varla möguleiki að ná þar fótfestu eða handfestu ef út af götunni kom, en hún gat verið tæp því í hana vildi renna aur ofan úr skriðunni. Alltaf var reynt að moka úr götunni, bæði fyrir menn og dýr, að sumrinu og á meðan jörð var ófrosin. Umferð var þar mikil, því kýr og hestar voru geymd í Skriðunum, en þar var allgott haglendi. Að vetrinum var oft farið þarna uppi undir klettum til þess að forðast snjóflóðahættu.

d8e369a2-f5cb-2030-589c-f8da035182e1.story_eng: Yngri-Upphagarétt, also called Yngri-Hrúthálsarétt, is the younger of two sheepfolds (rétt, a pen where sheep were gathered and sorted) built here. The older fold was used for only a short time. Jóhannes is said to have heard from his father Gissur that it was so hard to get the sheep into it that the farmers gave up on it. This fold was then built on the marsh, where it still stands. Both folds were used mainly for the spring round-ups. It is not known when the older fold was in use or when this one was built, but the last spring round-up sorted here was in the spring of 1978.
d8e369a2-f5cb-2030-589c-f8da035182e1.story_is: Upphagarétt eldri (Hrúthálsarétt eldri) var aðeins notuð í skamman tíma. Jóhannes hefur eftir Gissuri föður sínum að svo vont hafi verið að koma kindum inn í réttina að bændurnir gáfust upp á að nota hana. Þá var réttin byggð sem nú er á mýrinni, Upphagarétt yngri (Hrúthálsarétt yngri). Þessar réttir voru einkum notaðar við vorsmalanir. Ekki er vitað á hvaða árabili eldri réttin var notuð eða hvenær yngri réttin var byggð, en síðast var réttað vorsafni í Upphagarétt yngri vorið 1978.

d8efca8d-08f1-c551-1006-d45d53b1c2e5.story_eng: Gunnuhóll is a gravel mound south of Ytri-Grænur. According to oral tradition, a woman named Gunna died of exposure here, which is said to be how the hill got its name, meaning Gunna's hill.
d8efca8d-08f1-c551-1006-d45d53b1c2e5.story_is: Gunnuhóll heitir melur sunnan við Ytri-Grænur. Þar herma munnmæli að Gunna nokkur hafi orðið úti.

d8f4856a-c1cc-4322-97a9-a37c5c36c486.story_eng: People have climbed down into Syðri-Hælskora on a rope, just as they have into its neighbour, Ytri-Hælskora. Syðri-Hælskora lies between Kambsgjá and Bæjarlækur, the farm stream, while Ytri-Hælskora is just south of the stream.
d8f4856a-c1cc-4322-97a9-a37c5c36c486.story_is: Menn hafa farið niður á kaðli í Ytri-Hælskoru og Syðri-Hælskoru. Syðri-Hælskora er milli Kambsgjár og Bæjarlækjar, en sú ytri er rétt sunnan við Bæjarlækinn.

d8f7f470-6831-4452-1567-c4001d5b7708.story_eng: Niðurganga, meaning "the way down", is a path leading down to the shore, called Fjörur, at the northern end of Náttfaravíkur. The area is not known ever to have been used for anything but summer grazing for sheep. The sheep used this path to get down to the shore to graze. Shepherds also went down it to fetch the sheep when bad weather was expected, because the sheep were then at risk of being swept out to sea. The sheep stopped going down to the shore after the middle of the 20th century. By then there had been a collapse in this area, and new sheep that did not know the ground had been brought in after the flocks were replaced.
d8f7f470-6831-4452-1567-c4001d5b7708.story_is: Innanvert við Afréttarbolla eru Rauðunafir og þar er Niðurganga í Fjörur. Þetta er nyrst í Náttfaravíkum og er ekki vitað til þess að það svæði hafi nokkurn tímann verið nýtt til annars en sem afréttarland fyrir sauðfé. Niðurganga í Fjörur var farin af sauðfé sem leitaði í fjörubeitina. Leiðin var einnig farin af smalamönnum að sækja féð þegar von var á illviðrum, því þá var hætt við því að það tæki út. Sauðfé hætti að fara þarna niður í Fjörur eftir miðja síðustu öld, þegar hrun hafði orðið á þessu svæði og nýtt fé, sem var ókunnugt aðstæðum, kom á svæðið eftir fjárskiptin.

d8ffee28-175c-5639-2380-05e5efac4145.story_eng: Hveitibrauðshvammur means "wheat-bread hollow". A track runs through it that the people of Laxárdalur used when they travelled with pack-horse trains to Húsavík. Once they lost a sack of wholemeal flour off a horse here, and the hollow took its name from that event. It lies just above the dam.
d8ffee28-175c-5639-2380-05e5efac4145.story_is: Upp af stíflunni er Hveitibrauðshvammur. Um hann liggur gata sem Laxdælir fóru um þegar þeir fóru í lestarferðir til Húsavíkur. Eitt sinn misstu þeir heilhveitisekk af hesti í hvamminn og hlaut hann nafn sitt af þeim atburði.

d90a6d13-0f54-dcdf-a5c4-7a54592e7225.story_eng: This hill, just south of the old farm mound at Kollsvík and sometimes counted as part of it, is also known as Fjóshóll. It most likely held the small chapel (bænhús) that stood at Kollsvík in Catholic times. A stone near the top of the hill, on its south side, is said to be one of the foundations of the churchyard wall. After the Reformation, livestock houses were probably built on the hill, as often happened at former Catholic church sites. In the first half of the 20th century a barn called Langahlaða (the long barn) stood here. Its name later changed to Jónshlaða, after Jón Torfason, a farmer in Kollsvík. A cowshed stood beside the barn, and a concrete pit was later built a short distance away. When it was being dug, human bones came up from the old churchyard, and more bones were found later in a vegetable garden that long lay on the west side of the hill. Further south on the hill are sheep houses and their hay barns.
d90a6d13-0f54-dcdf-a5c4-7a54592e7225.story_is: Jónshlaða, eða Fjóshóll, er heiti á hól og útihúsum á honum, sunnan gamla Bæjarhólsins í Kollsvík; stundum talið hluti af honum. Á þessum hól stóð að öllum líkindum bænhús það sem var í Kollsvík í kaþólskum sið. Steinn er í hólnum ofanverðum, sunnan til, og fylgir sú saga að hann sé ein af undirstöðum kirkjugarðsins. Eftir siðaskipti hafa líklega verið reist skepnuhús á hólnum, líkt og oft var um kirkjustaði úr pápísku. Á fyrri hluta 20. aldar stóð þar svokölluð Langahlaða. Nafn hennar breyttist síðar í Jónshlaða, í höfuðið á Jóni Torfasyni, bónda í Kollsvík. Hjá hlöðunni var fjós, og stutt frá henni var síðar reist steypt gryfja. Þegar grafið var fyrir henni komu upp mannabein úr kirkjugarðinum sem þarna var. Bein hafa komið upp síðar, í kálgarði sem lengi var vestan í hólnum. Sunnar á hólnum eru fjárhús og fjárhúshlöður.

d9202c57-71b3-6728-5f51-71f709192b02.story_eng: Hestklettur (horse rock) is a rock on the gravel banks along the east side of the river Héraðsvötn, about 150–200 metres north of the site of the old cable ferry, Kláfurinn. According to stories, 62 years before Kláfurinn existed, a kind of cable ferry was set up across Héraðsvötn. In 1817 the farmer Jón Einarsson is said to have strung a rope across the river and carried his household goods over on it when he moved from Ánastaðir to Tyrfingsstaðir. The poet Jónas Hallgrímsson wrote a poem about this crossing, and in it he names Hestklettur. The rope crossing was probably somewhat further south, below Villinganes. If it was here at Hestklettur, it too was on the land of Lýtingsstaðir.
d9202c57-71b3-6728-5f51-71f709192b02.story_is: Hestklettur er klettur í eyrum vestan Grænamós, við Vötnin austanverð, um 150–200 metrum norðan við Kláfsstæðið. Sagnir eru um að 62 árum fyrir daga Kláfsins hafi einskonar kláfferja verið sett á Héraðsvötn, en líklega hefur hún verið nokkru sunnar, heldur suður og niður frá Villinganesi. Hefur þá Jón bóndi Einarsson sett seil yfir Vötnin árið 1817 og ferjað búslóð sína yfir á henni, er hann flutti búferlum frá Ánastöðum í Tyrfingsstaði. Um þetta hefur Jónas Hallgrímsson gert kvæði og þar nefnir hann Hestklett. Hafi Seilin verið þar hefur hún einnig verið úr landi Lýtingsstaða.

d9285e6e-49b1-5a7e-da71-fcc24c244657.story_eng: Leiti is a fairly large grassy rise below Hæð. For anyone coming home along Traðarhæð, it is at Leiti that the old farm mound, Bæjarhóllinn, comes into view. In front of Leiti lies a fairly large stone called Hvíldarsteinn, the resting stone. People rested there on their way home from pulling heather, which in former times was gathered for firewood.
d9285e6e-49b1-5a7e-da71-fcc24c244657.story_is: Leiti er allstórt graslendi sunnan við Tröð, ofan við Buga, uppundir Hæð. Þegar komið er heim með Traðarhæðinni sést heim að gamla Bæjarhólnum á Leitinu. Fyrir framan Leiti er allstór steinn sem heitir Hvíldarsteinn. Þar hvíldi fólk sig þegar komið var heim úr lyngrifi. Áður fyrr var lyng rifið til eldiviðar.

d92fa3bd-90c5-3710-bc3d-ae2018688955.story_eng: Huldusteinn is a very large, solitary stone lying beneath Sveigsbarði, a high eroded bank facing south on a wind-stripped gravel plain at the edge of a ravine. The old track Sveigsgötur ran across this plain. Many people believed that huldufólk (hidden people, the elf-like beings of Icelandic folk belief) lived in the stone, which is reflected in its name, meaning hidden stone.
d92fa3bd-90c5-3710-bc3d-ae2018688955.story_is: Á giljaðrinum lágu Sveigsgötur um uppblásinn mel með háu rofbarði móti suðri, Sveigsbarði. Undir því er ákaflega stór, stakur steinn, Huldusteinn. Þar hugðu ýmsir huldufólk búa.

d931a67e-6100-45e1-8af1-794985d50632.story_eng: Bæjarstæði, whose name means "farm site", lies to the south by the river branch Hrúteyjarkvísl, just east of Brúarstæði. Large turf walls and the ruins of buildings remain there. Oral tradition says the farm once had 18 doors hung on iron hinges.
d931a67e-6100-45e1-8af1-794985d50632.story_is: Bæjarstæði er suður við Hrúteyjarkvísl, rétt austan við Brúarstæði. Eru þar miklir garðar og húsarústir og herma munnmæli að þar hafi verið 18 hurðir á járnum.

d9425124-5897-0ccc-4e39-51a553524e71.story_eng: Nibba is the foremost part of Blakkur, high up on its edge, and in some places it is called Blakknesnibba. Fulmars (múkki) nest here in great numbers, and people used to go for their eggs along the highest ledges. On Nibba is a spot called Kollsleiði (leiði means grave). A cleft called Nibbugjá offers a way down to Sighvatsstóð.
d9425124-5897-0ccc-4e39-51a553524e71.story_is: Nibba er fremsti hluti Blakks, uppi á brún, og er sums staðar nefnd Blakknesnibba. Múkki verpur þar mikið og var farið til eggja í efstu göngum. Á Nibbu er Kollsleiði. Um Nibbugjá er farið niður í Sighvatsstóð.

d95b7017-7ff0-7545-98d1-43c5bc559e98.story_eng: Kotafjara had a shelter called Byrgi, which was probably a sjóbúð, a fishermen's hut used during the fishing season. Another shelter here, a shooting hide, was named after Kotamýrar-Finni, but the stream has since washed it away. Nothing remains of the fishing hut. It has probably been lost to the sea eating away at the land, or buried under the stones of the shore. One badly eroded ruin can still be made out. It is said to be the remains of a beitarhús, a sheep house out in the grazing land, with a feeding trough. The shore is strewn with large boulders and some driftwood. It lies about 750 m northeast of the farm.
d95b7017-7ff0-7545-98d1-43c5bc559e98.story_is: Í Kotafjöru er Byrgi sem sennilega hefur verið sjóbúð. Annað skotbyrgi var þar kennt við Kotamýrar-Finna en það hefur lækurinn nú eytt. Ekkert sér til minja um sjóbúðina, sem hefur að líkindum horfið vegna landbrots af völdum sjávar eða grafist undir grjóti í fjörunni. Ein tóft, illa farin af landbroti, er þó greinanleg í fjörunni og er sögð leifar af beitarhúsum með garða. Í fjörunni er mikið um hnullungagrjót og eitthvað af rekaviði. Kotafjara er um 750 m norðaustan við bæinn.

d969297a-c3e8-e205-c0ee-539d526c2319.story_eng: Rósukofar ("Rósa's huts") are the fragments of old ruins just west of, below the rock outcrop called Sker. It is said that there was once a farm here, named after an old woman called Rósa. The remains are overgrown with grass and seem very old, and they have become indistinct, though the buildings were probably fairly large. The spot has stayed greener than the land around it. There may have been a small homefield, and faint traces of a homefield wall can be seen to the northwest.
d969297a-c3e8-e205-c0ee-539d526c2319.story_is: Vestan undir Skerinu eru tóftarbrot sem heita Rósukofar. Er sagt að þar hafi verið býli og kennt við kerlingu sem Rósa hét. Þar hefur verið blettur grænni en umhverfið. Mannvirkjaleifarnar eru vallgrónar og virðast vera mjög gamlar og ógreinilegar orðnar, en líklega hafa verið þarna tiltölulega stór hús. Túnblettur getur hafa verið dálítill og ógreinilegar leifar af túngarði sjást norðvestan við.

d971d7ff-0f1c-3b57-b98a-89e7f9880c27.story_eng: Birga, also called Birguhóll, is a fairly high mound. It is said that a hidden woman, one of the huldufólk (hidden people), once lived there. The last human to live there was an old woman named Birgitta, or Birgit. The dwelling no longer exists.
